stories.title: Elon Musk says 'unsustainably high' costs are the reason for Grok Bot usage limits
stories.summary: The SpaceX CEO said the cost of serving the AI agent was "unsustainably high relative to revenue," after some users complained about usage limits.

sources.name: TechRadar
sources.title: Elon Musk says Grok Bot was throttled as costs were ‘unsustainably high’
sources.text: If you noticed that you burned through your Grok Bot usage much faster than usual in recent days, there’s a reason for that: Elon Musk intentionally limited users’ AI agent allowances in the face of “unsustainably high costs.” And as you’d expect, a lot of people are unhappy with that. The revelation came about after an X user pinged platform owner Musk , asking for a Grok Bot reset after they surprisingly hit their 100% usage limit, four days before it was due to reset. They additionally commented that “Normally I don’t even reach 100%.” Musk then replied to the post , stating: “The cost of serving Grok Bot was unsustainably high relative to revenue.” Many X users seemed irked by the situation, with several saying that their Grok Bot usage had hit the 100% limit while they were sleeping and not using any AI agents. Users claimed their usage had suddenly gone from 50% to 100%, 35% to 78%, and 70% to 100%, all supposedly without using Grok Bot at all. Elon Musk’s comments come amid broader scrutiny of the financial sustainability of many AI products. Tech stocks — including those of many leading AI firms — fell sharply last week as investors grew concerned over the profitability of the industry , with Google revealing that its own AI summaries have hurt its search advertising revenue. Concerns have also been raised in recent months over the finances involved in many AI companies’ offerings. For instance, users of AI tools like ChatGPT and Claude Code can often spend many times more in tokens than they’re actually paying in monthly subscriptions, leading to questions over how sustainable many AI business models really are and whether things will need to be adjusted in the near future. This changing landscape hasn’t gone down well with many users, of course. One thread on Reddit dubbed Musk’s about-face an “indirect rug pull” of Grok Bot, with features and usage limited in a bid to cut costs. Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more. But it’s unlikely that AI producers will be able to subsidize their products’ costs to users forever. Usage limits will necessarily need to tighten (as OpenAI quietly announced recently, much to the frustration of users ) and prices will need to increase for these business models to make sense. So don’t be surprised if Grok Bot’s lower cap is just the first of many big changes looming on the horizon. stories.title: Meta Partners With Five US Universities to Accelerate Medical and Scientific Breakthroughs
stories.summary: Meta is bringing Superintelligence models, research funding, and direct researcher collaboration to US universities that are using our models to solve critical issues in science and medicine. The post Meta Partners With Five US Universities to Accelerate Medical and Scientific Breakthroughs appeared first on Meta Newsroom .

sources.name: Meta Newsroom
sources.title: Meta Partners With Five US Universities to Accelerate Medical and Scientific Breakthroughs
sources.text: We believe the future is for everyone, including America’s universities, professors, students, and the communities who benefit from their research. That’s why Meta is bringing Superintelligence models, research funding, and direct researcher collaboration to academia through partnerships with five US universities: California Institute of Technology, The Ohio State University College of Medicine, Louisiana State University, Indiana University, and UTHealth Houston. We’re expanding our academic partnerships by granting $2 million across these five schools to support research that uses our models to accelerate breakthroughs in medicine, physics, chemistry, biology, computer science, and mathematics. In medicine and healthcare, researchers will work on a diverse set of projects using Meta’s models, glasses, and mixed reality headsets to address existing gaps in medicine and healthcare. Here are a few examples of how they’re being used: When tracheostomy tubes become dislodged in infant patients, it’s a life-threatening emergency compounded by the fact that babies with tracheostomies can’t cry out for help. And continuous direct observation by trained staff isn’t always possible. Dr. Michael Dunham from Louisiana State University is leading the Eyes-On project, which is developing a computer vision system to continuously detect tracheostomy tube displacement and signs of distress in infants who cannot reliably vocalize. The system is exploring usage of our open weight SAM models for tracking and is designed for integration with bedside cameras and edge computing. A proof-of-concept has been published, with more work to come. People with dementia often experience communication difficulties that standard conversational AI systems handle poorly, leading to frustration rather than support. Dr. David Crandall at Indiana University is developing a project that aims to develop multimodal AI methods for analyzing conversations involving older adults living with dementia, and to use this understanding to help conversational agents — including social robots — adapt their interactions to individual users. The research tests whether AI systems can be made sensitive to the communication patterns of people with cognitive differences. Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) accounts for roughly half of all heart failure cases, but it can be difficult to recognize early — its symptoms overlap with those of obesity and other common conditions, so formal evaluation often begins only after clinical suspicion has developed. At The Ohio State University College of Medicine, AI researcher Dr. Yuan Xue is leading a project with cardiologist Dr. Yuchi Han and AI researcher Dr. Xia Ning to investigate how Meta’s open-weight models can help predict future HFpEF risk using routine abdominal CT scans, longitudinal medical records, and ECG data when available. The team is designing the model to handle missing data, since real-world clinical practice rarely provides a complete set of inputs. You can read more on these projects on our Research Blog , and we look forward to sharing more as these projects get underway.

stories.title: Train, Evaluate, and Deploy Anomaly Detection Models with Roboflow
stories.summary: Train an anomaly detection model in Roboflow on images of good products only, and get a heatmap of every defect it finds.

sources.name: Roboflow
sources.title: Train, Evaluate, and Deploy Anomaly Detection Models with Roboflow
sources.text: Today we’re announcing full support for anomaly detection models (opens in a new tab) in Roboflow, allowing you to deploy them in the cloud or on your hardware. Anomaly detection allows you to find things that look different from normal, like a damaged component or a stray bolt on a conveyor belt, without needing images of those issues to train on. That way, you can build vision systems that catch rare, unpredictable problems, even without examples of them in your training data. An anomaly detection model is trained on images that show what "good" looks like. Then, when you run new images through the model, it tells you whether each one is normal or anomalous, returns an anomaly score, and can produce a heatmap of the areas that differ the most. Anomalies are, by definition, hard to find. On a well-run production line, a defect might show up once in thousands of parts, and no two look the same. Collecting enough labeled examples to train an object detection or classification model takes a long time. That makes anomaly detection a great fit for quality assurance and quality control (QA/QC), like sorting food, inspecting parts and packaging, and catching defects you couldn’t list in advance. The model can return the anomaly "severity" in the form of a heatmap. In the above video of an anomaly detection model running on this egg line, the model flags stains, chips, and marks on the shell. Yellow indicates the anomaly is slightly above the threshold, while red indicates an anomaly far above it. Here is another example where we trained FoundAD on frames of rocks, and it flags a stray bolt and a piece of debris it didn't see during training. In this case, we're using SAHI (Slicing Aided Hyper Inference), then feeding each slice separately to the anomaly detection model. Object detection needs labeled examples of every defect you want to find. On a production line that's the hard part: defects are rare, and every one looks different. A scratch, a dent, a missing screw and a stain have little in common, except that none of them look like a good part. Anomaly detection flips that. Good parts are easy to collect, so the model learns from those and flags the rest. It works well for: It's also a good first model when you have no defect data yet . Run it on the line, review what it flags, and you have the start of a labeled defect dataset for an object detection model later. Both architectures start from an image model pre-trained on millions of images, and use it to describe every small patch of your image. Either way you get an anomaly score for the image and an (optional) heatmap of where it came from. We trained both on four categories of the VisA dataset (opens in a new tab) , once with 4 normal images and once with all of them. FoundAD is the better pick when you only have a few good images, in line with the FoundAD paper (opens in a new tab) . More data helps both, PatchCore the most. FoundAD’s speed doesn’t depend on how many images you train on. PatchCore searches a memory bank that grows with the training set, so it slows down as you add data. Which of the two is faster depends on the hardware. Resolution matters even more, since both the patches per image and the memory bank grow with it: So for higher-resolution inputs, FoundAD is usually more applicable. PatchCore trains in minutes, while FoundAD takes longer (hours on large datasets). Each model ran at its default image size (224×224 for PatchCore, 512×512 for FoundAD) on Roboflow Inference 1.8, using the public Jetson image on the Jetsons. We measured it using inference-cli (opens in a new tab) ( inference benchmark api-speed ): 10 warm-up requests, then 100 timed ones per model, sent one at a time. These results come from one benchmark, so treat them as an example, not as what to expect. Accuracy and speed on your data depend on your images, defects, image size, and hardware, so try both models on your own data. In app.roboflow.com , click "New Project" and pick "Anomaly Detection" as the project type. Upload images of good products and label them "normal". The model trains on these only, so normal images are all you need to get started. If you have some anomalous images, you can label them "anomalous" and they won't be used to train the model (both architectures learn from normal images only, and anomalous images in the training split are skipped). They will be used to pick the threshold that best separates normal from anomalous, and to report precision and recall. Without them, it sets the threshold from the normal validation images, so roughly 1% of them would be flagged. Labels are per image: open an image from "Annotate" and pick "normal" or "anomalous", like a classification model. If there's an anomalous object, you don't mark where the defect is; the model works that out on its own and returns it as a heatmap (see Step 4). Most of your images will be normal, so you can label a whole upload batch at once with "Mark All Normal". Our final dataset had 962 normal crops for training, plus 208 validation images (12 anomalous) and 130 test images (11 anomalous) to set the threshold and check accuracy. Click "Train Model", pick an architecture, and choose the dataset version to train on. We trained both on the same version. On our test set PatchCore came out ahead: it caught 14 of 15 real defects at 2 false alarms, while FoundAD caught 10. PatchCore trains in minutes and FoundAD takes longer (see the benchmark above), so try both on your data. When training finishes, the model shows up under "Models". Send it an image through the Serverless API, and add include_anomaly_map to get the heatmap back: The response has anomaly_score , anomaly_threshold and is_anomalous , plus the heatmap at the model's input resolution. Create an Anomaly Detection project, upload images of good parts, and train your first model today. Sign up for Roboflow to get started, or talk to sales about running it across your lines.
